extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and informed citizens studying American government/civics
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing the constitutional powers, limits, and internal procedures of the U.S. Congress (including impeachment, control of executive and judicial branches, party organization, House rules, and committee privileges). Intended to teach how Congress works in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright administration practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration of the copyright law is in the hands of the registrar of copyrights, who works under the direction of the librarian of Congress. Every applicant receives his copyright, for no attempt is made by the division of copyrights to examine into questions of infringement as in the case of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: registration is ministerial — issuance does not involve substantive examination for infringement; reference: Report of Copyright Legislation (1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal power and federal control of mail transportation
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment of post-offices and post-roads is exclusively a federal matter, and the power of the federal government covers the whole domain of mail transportation, within each state as well as among the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat postal establishment and mail transport as within exclusive federal authority, closely related to commerce power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign commerce and related foreign-relations powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may regulate foreign commerce, including the important branch of immigration; create consular and diplomatic posts abroad and provide the emoluments thereunto attached; define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas and offences against the law of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes power to establish a uniform naturalization rule (exclusive to Congress), though states may nonetheless confer voting rights on aliens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive federal authority over the monetary system
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation of the monetary system is vested exclusively in the federal legislature. Congress has power to coin money, regulate its value, and the value of foreign coin. States are forbidden to coin money, emit bills of credit, or make anything but the gold and silver coin of the United States a tender in the payment of debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Constitution does not expressly authorize paper money, Congress has exercised that power and been sustained by Supreme Court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on congressional power to define crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of Congress to define crimes and provide punishments for them is narrowly limited. Treason is expressly defined in the Constitution; Congress cannot make any offence which it chooses treason. Congress may define crimes against federal laws duly passed under the terms of the Constitution, although it has no power of defining crime in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may punish federal offenses (e.g., theft connected with mail) but general criminal lawmaking is left to the states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authority over territories, districts, and federal property
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of the territories and districts belonging to the United States is vested in the federal authorities. Congress has the power to dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States, to exercise exclusive legislation in all cases whatsoever over the District of Columbia, and over all places purchased by the federal government (with the consent of the state legislatures concerned) for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exercising authority over territories, Congress combines federal and state-like powers but remains subject to constitutional limitations (e.g., cannot establish press censorship or official religion); power to admit new states and supervise organization of territories is vested in Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper Clause interpreted broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: In carrying into execution the powers vested by the Constitution ... Congress may make all laws which shall be deemed 'necessary and proper.' The courts have, in general, given a liberal interpretation to this phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance (Juilhard v. Greenman): 'The words 'necessary and proper' are not limited to such measures as are absolutely and indispensably necessary ... they include all the proper means which are conducive or adapted to the end to be accomplished and which, in the judgment of Congress, will most advantageously effect it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional control over executive departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may determine the number of executive departments and provide for the internal organization of each; it may regulate even the minutest duties of Cabinet officers and exercise substantial dominion over executive departments under its power to tax salaries and define duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of control over President's personal advisers is disputed, but statutory powers over organization, duties, and salaries give Congress levers of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power over the federal judiciary's structure and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may determine the number of Supreme Court judges, fix their salaries (subject to certain limits), and define their appellate jurisdiction. The creation of inferior federal courts is subject to its power; and it may define the jurisdiction and procedure of these courts and provide the methods by which cases may be drawn from the state courts into the federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Judiciary Act of 1789 provided mechanisms for bringing state statutes into federal courts and testing their validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prescribe full faith and credit mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has the power of providing the precise manner in which the acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each state shall be given full faith and credit in every other state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative prescriptions can define how states' records and judgments are recognized across state lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment: House prosecution and Senate trial procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of preferring and prosecuting charges against offenders is vested in the House of Representatives. In trying cases of impeachment, the Senate acts as the high court. When the President is being tried, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court presides. It requires a two-thirds vote of the members present to convict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: House adopts articles of impeachment, chooses managers/prosecutors, conducts the case similarly to an ordinary trial; conviction threshold = two-thirds present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment penalties and post-conviction liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The penalty which the Senate can impose upon any person convicted in case of impeachment is strictly limited to the removal of the offender from office and the imposition of a disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States. Any person convicted, however, is still liable, after his removal from office, to indictment, trial, judgment, and punishment for his offence according to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate may but is not obliged to disqualify from future federal service; removal is mandatory on conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and exclusions of impeachment jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the Senate as a court of impeachment extends only over the President, Vice-President, and the civil officers of the United States, and over the offences of treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors. Federal military officers are exempt (subject to courts-martial). Members of Congress are not 'civil officers' and are under the control of their respective houses, which may punish disorderly behavior and, with the concurrence of two-thirds, expel a member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different remedies/processes apply to different categories of officials: courts-martial for military, internal house discipline/expulsion for members of Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive norm for 'other high crimes and misdemeanors'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'other high crimes and misdemeanors' is somewhat vague, and Congress might give a loose interpretation to it ... Nevertheless, a conservative interpretation has generally been placed upon this phrase, so as to limit the offences which render an officer liable to impeachment to crimes and misdemeanors as understood in the ordinary law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/practical guidance favors limiting impeachment to conduct that would be regarded as crimes or misdemeanors in ordinary law rather than purely political disagreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party organization and caucus role in congressional working methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The working methods of Congress are largely determined by the existence of two political parties. Each party in the Senate and the House is organized into a congressional caucus, in which is frequently determined the line of party action with regard to important legislative questions. The caucus chooses the Speaker and party leaders and decides whether to adopt or modify the rules of the preceding Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caucuses are organized under rules members are expected to abide by; influence varies over time and may decline as powerful leaders and committee chairs gain control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member freedom to introduce bills and consequence of log-rolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Any member may introduce as many bills as he pleases by handing them to the clerk (private) or to the Speaker (public); he does not have to secure permission in advance even though they may involve heavy charges upon the public treasury. This practice is largely responsible for extravagance and confusion and for the 'log-rolling' process in which national interests are subordinated to local interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: enormous legislative workload, predominance of local/pork-barrel measures, and pressure on House to select which measures to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of business concentrated in majority leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to select from the enormous mass before the House must be vested in the hands of some person or group of persons (leaders). In the House these leaders are the Speaker, the committee on rules, and the chairmen of the principal committees to which bills are referred; the rules provide ways by which they can make selections of business for consideration and limit debate time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: majority leadership (Speaker, rules committee, committee chairs) control the House's agenda and pace of business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's authority to refuse purely dilatory motions (Reed Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker of the House may refuse to put motions which he regards as dilatory: that is, designed merely to delay business. This principle was established by Speaker Reed and later embodied in the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive note: the constitutional right of a member to demand the yeas and nays cannot be denied even if the purpose is dilatory; Reed defended the ruling as necessary to enable action rather than stoppage of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting as present members who refuse to answer roll-call
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker may count as present those members who are physically present but refuse to answer to their names on a roll-call for the purpose of compelling an adjournment in the absence of a quorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established by Speaker Reed and incorporated in the rules to prevent quorum obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic limit on debate time per member
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules provide a method for automatically shortening debate by prescribing that the time occupied by any member in discussing a legislative proposition shall not exceed one hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member may yield part of his time to others; may not speak twice on same measure unless he introduced it or reports it from committee; committee of the whole fixes debate time which cannot be extended by the committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged reporting rights of certain committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain committees may report on the subjects enumerated practically at any time in the course of the procedure of the House: e.g., the committee on rules (rules, joint rules, order of business); the committee on elections (right of a member to his seat); the committee on ways and means (bills raising revenue); committees having jurisdiction of appropriations (general appropriations bills); committee on rivers and harbors (improvement bills); committee on public lands (forfeiture of land grants, reservation of public lands); committee on territories (admission of new states); committee on enrolled bills; committee on invalid pensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These privileged reporting rights enable party leaders to force consideration of certain measures whenever they see fit and give procedural advantage to bills within committee jurisdictions.
